strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Evaluating memory capabilities in reinforcement learning has historically relied on fragmented, often navigation- or gridworld-based benchmarks, leaving robotic manipulation largely under-explored despite real-world partial observability.
Clear taxonomy: Categorizing memory-intensive tasks into Object Memory, Spatial Memory, Sequential Memory, and Memory Capacity provides a structured conceptual framing inspired by cognitive science.

Comprehensive robotic task suite (MIKASA-Robo): The design of 32 tabletop manipulation tasks in ManiSkill3 across multiple modalities (vector state, RGB, joint proprioception) and difficulty tiers is a valuable addition to the community.
Sound sanity validation: Demonstrating 100% success rate with PPO-MLP under fully observable state mode confirms that the tasks are physically and kinematically solvable.
weaknesses: Extremely limited baseline evaluation: In a benchmark specifically introduced to evaluate memory-enhanced RL agents, only vanilla LSTM is tested against a memory-less MLP. Modern memory architectures—such as Transformers (e.g., GTrXL, Decision Transformer variants), State Space Models (e.g., S5, Mamba), and retrieval/episodic memory mechanisms—are completely omitted.

Incomplete empirical evaluation across the suite: Out of the 32 proposed MIKASA-Robo tasks, the main body only highlights a single task (RememberColor), while the appendix evaluates only a subset (~12 tasks) with PPO-LSTM/MLP. A benchmark paper should provide a comprehensive performance table or aggregate metrics across the entire suite.

MIKASA-Base offers limited technical novelty: MIKASA-Base is primarily an aggregation and Gymnasium standardization wrapper for pre-existing benchmarks (POPGym, MemoryGym, BSuite, etc.), with no new algorithmic or architectural insights.

Writing and presentation defects: The abstract ends with an incomplete, truncated sentence ('The code is available a'). Furthermore, the main paper defers almost all baseline learning curves and environment details to the appendix, leaving Section 6.3 notably thin.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap: while memory benchmarks exist for 2D grids and 3D navigation, standardized benchmarks evaluating memory capabilities in continuous robotic manipulation tasks are scarce.
Proposes a clear, cognitively grounded four-part taxonomy (Object Memory, Spatial Memory, Sequential Memory, Memory Capacity) to categorize memory-intensive RL environments.
MIKASA-Robo provides a diverse suite of 32 tabletop manipulation tasks built on ManiSkill3, leveraging modern GPU-parallelized simulation with standardized Gymnasium interfaces.

Sound validation methodology: the oracle/state-mode experiments demonstrate that all tasks are dynamically feasible and solvable with 100% success rate, ensuring that failures in partial observability stem from memory/perception rather than environment mechanics.
weaknesses: Very limited baseline evaluation: The empirical study evaluates only PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM. While comparing an RNN to a reactive MLP is a reasonable sanity check, a contemporary benchmark paper should benchmark modern memory architectures (e.g., GTrXL, Decision Transformer, AMAGO, or SSM/Mamba-based RL agents) that are highlighted throughout the paper's own taxonomy and related works.

No empirical results for MIKASA-Base: Although MIKASA-Base is introduced as a major contribution to unify existing POMDP benchmarks, the paper does not provide cross-benchmark baseline experiments or unified empirical comparisons on this suite.

Task diversity in manipulation dynamics is somewhat restricted: Several tasks (e.g., RememberColor, RememberShape, SeqOfColors, BunchOfColors, ChainOfColors) largely decouple memory from manipulation—the agent essentially observes a visual stimulus and then performs a simple reach/touch action on static objects, functioning more as visual memory tests wrapped in a robotic setting rather than deeply interactive manipulation.

Noticeable presentation and drafting issues: The abstract abruptly cuts off mid-sentence ('The code is available a'), Section 6 ends with an incomplete sentence ('To fill this gap, we introduce the MIKASA-Robo framework for the RL.'), and Figure 1 contains unfilled placeholder rectangles in text bubbles.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing an important problem: assessing memory capabilities in RL within continuous robotic manipulation, where benchmark tasks with realistic partial observability and temporal dependencies have been relatively scarce.

The benchmark suite MIKASA-Robo introduces 32 diverse manipulation tasks implemented on top of the GPU-parallelized ManiSkill3 simulator, spanning several task types (object tracking, visual attribute matching, spatial prediction, and sequential ordering).

Thorough sanity checks in the oracle state mode demonstrate that the MIKASA-Robo tasks are kinematically and dynamically solvable (achieving 100% success rate with PPO-MLP when full state information is provided).
Extensive appendix documentation covering task descriptions, reward definitions, and environment wrappers.
weaknesses: Critically limited baseline evaluation: Despite extensive review of modern memory architectures in the literature (e.g., Transformers such as GTrXL, State Space Models like S4/S5/Mamba, and retrieval-augmented RL), the experimental evaluation only evaluates PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM. A benchmark paper should establish competitive baselines representing modern memory architectures to demonstrate its utility.

Absence of experimental results for MIKASA-Base: Although MIKASA-Base is claimed as one of the paper's three main contributions, the manuscript presents no empirical evaluation or baseline comparisons across this unified suite.

Conflation of visual control difficulty and memory retention: In MIKASA-Robo (RGB+joints), PPO-LSTM struggles significantly even on modest variants. In vision-based robotic manipulation, sample complexity and exploration challenges with on-policy algorithms like PPO often cause policy collapse irrespective of memory capacity. Without stronger off-policy baselines or demonstrations, it remains ambiguous whether agents fail due to memory constraints or standard visual RL optimization bottlenecks.

Limited novelty in task categorization: The proposed four-category taxonomy (Object, Spatial, Sequential, Capacity) is largely derived from standard cognitive psychology and previous classification frameworks (e.g., Cherepanov et al., 2024a; Morad et al., 2023), offering modest conceptual novelty.
Presentation and writing polish: The abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('The code is available a'), reflecting incomplete editing prior to submission.

strengths: Clear motivation and taxonomy: The paper addresses a significant fragmentation in evaluating memory in RL by establishing a coherent taxonomy (Object, Spatial, Sequential, Capacity) grounded in cognitive science.

Comprehensive robotic manipulation suite: Introducing MIKASA-Robo with 32 tasks across 12 distinct categories built on ManiSkill3 provides a valuable, GPU-parallelized, standardized platform for studying POMDPs in continuous control.

Sound validation of task solvability: By training oracle state-based PPO agents that achieve 100% success rates, the authors convincingly establish that the tasks are physically solvable and that agent failures under RGB observations are due to memory/POMDP challenges rather than physical impossibility.

Diverse experimental paradigms: The evaluation covers classic Online RL (PPO, SAC, TD-MPC2), sequence-oriented and diffusion-based Offline RL (DT, RATE, Diffusion Policy, CQL, BC), and modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Octo, OpenVLA).
Open-source usability: Providing pre-collected offline datasets and simple installation (`pip install mikasa-robo-suite`) supports reproducibility and ease of adoption by the community.
weaknesses: Short temporal horizons: The memory retention delays in many tasks are relatively brief (e.g., 5-step delay phases in RememberColor, occlusion occurring at step 5 with episode lengths between 60-180 steps). While suitable for short-term working memory, the suite does not heavily probe long-horizon or persistent memory over hundreds or thousands of steps.

Artificial mechanics in several tasks: In several tasks (e.g., RememberColor, RememberShape, SeqOfColors), objects artificially disappear and reappear rather than experiencing natural occlusions or physical relocations, which somewhat limits the ecological realism of the manipulation setting.

Limited online memory baselines: The online RL experiments only compare an MLP against an LSTM backbone (alongside SAC and TD-MPC2), omitting modern online memory architectures such as GTrXL, AMAGO, or State-Space Models (S4/Mamba), which would provide a clearer ceiling of current memory-RL methods.

Scope of MIKASA-Base: MIKASA-Base is primarily an API wrapper around previously established benchmarks (POPGym, MemoryGym, BSuite, etc.) rather than a newly designed contribution, making MIKASA-Robo the primary novel environment contribution.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in reinforcement learning and robot manipulation: evaluating memory capabilities in continuous, physical control settings rather than purely discrete gridworlds or 3D navigation.
Well-structured taxonomy categorizing memory demands into four distinct types (Object Memory, Spatial Memory, Sequential Memory, and Memory Capacity) grounded in cognitive science principles.
The MIKASA-Robo suite is implemented on top of ManiSkill3, leveraging GPU-accelerated simulation which makes training and evaluating deep RL agents computationally tractable.

Thorough sanity checks and diagnostic validation: the authors demonstrate that all tasks are 100% solvable under full state (MDP) observability using PPO-MLP, confirming that the task dynamics, physical interactions, and reward structures are valid and well-calibrated.

Extensive baseline comparisons covering Online RL (PPO-MLP, PPO-LSTM, SAC, TD-MPC2), Offline RL (BC, CQL, Decision Transformer, RATE, Diffusion Policy), and Vision-Language-Action models (Octo, OpenVLA), alongside the release of offline demonstration datasets and a pip-installable package.
weaknesses: While MIKASA-Base unifies diverse existing memory environments under a common Gymnasium API, its conceptual novelty is somewhat limited as it primarily aggregates and standardizes existing benchmarks (e.g., POPGym, Memory Gym, bsuite).

Many manipulation tasks in MIKASA-Robo (e.g., colored cubes appearing, disappearing, and reappearing) are stylized cognitive probes transposed into a robot manipulation setup, which somewhat diverges from natural physical occlusions and continuous interactions encountered in real-world manipulation.

Several complex offline RL benchmark tasks show near-total failure across all baseline methods (0.00% success rate on BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors), leaving little signal to distinguish relative model quality on those specific sub-benchmarks without more granular intermediate metrics.

Evaluation on VLA models (Octo and OpenVLA) is restricted to only three task families with relatively limited fine-tuning (e.g., fine-tuning readout heads or LoRA on small demo sets), though this limitation is openly acknowledged by the authors.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in the robot learning literature: while memory and POMDP benchmarks exist for abstract gridworlds and navigation, standardized memory-intensive robotic manipulation benchmarks remain scarce.

The benchmark suite MIKASA-Robo introduces 32 GPU-accelerated tasks built on ManiSkill3 across 12 categories, categorized into four cognitive memory classes (Object, Spatial, Sequential, and Capacity memory).

Thorough sanity and solvability check: the authors demonstrate that all tasks achieve a 100% success rate under full state observability with PPO-MLP, verifying that the difficulty under partial observability stems from memory/perception demands rather than physical unsolvability.

Comprehensive empirical baseline coverage spanning multiple paradigms: on-policy and off-policy online RL (PPO-MLP/LSTM, SAC, TD-MPC2), offline RL (BC, CQL, DT, RATE, Diffusion Policy), and foundation VLA models (Octo, OpenVLA).
High reproducibility and practical community utility with released datasets (1000 trajectories per task) and an installable Python package.
weaknesses: Severe floor effect on several task suites: As reported in Table 6, nearly all offline RL algorithms achieve exactly 0.00% success rate on Memory Capacity (BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors) and Sequential Memory (ChainOfColors) tasks. While this demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty, near-zero performance across baselines offers limited discriminative ability to compare current algorithmic trade-offs.

Synthetic nature of many manipulation tasks: A large fraction of the MIKASA-Robo tasks involve abstract memory games adapted to a tabletop (e.g., colored cubes appearing, disappearing, and being touched in order) rather than organic, physically grounded memory challenges such as searching through cluttered drawers or performing multi-stage continuous tool assembly.

MIKASA-Base has limited technical novelty: It primarily unifies and wraps existing benchmarks (POPGym, MemoryGym, MiniGrid, BSuite) under Gymnasium rather than introducing novel conceptual formulations or environments.

Narrow exploration of specialized memory architectures: While LSTM, DT, and RATE are evaluated, modern long-sequence or structured memory models (such as selective state-space models like Mamba/S5 or explicit episodic memory buffers) are not benchmarked, which would have provided deeper insights into architectural solutions for these tasks.

VLA evaluation is constrained: Due to computational budgets, only a small subset of tasks and restricted fine-tuning configurations were tested for Octo and OpenVLA, leaving open questions regarding the scalability of larger multimodal backbones.
